zh:
我本该死在那一日的。
在那日之前，我是江南最负盛名的商贾上官家最受宠爱的嫡小姐。爹爹日日将我捧在手心，只要我开口，哪怕是天上的月亮，他也愿意去为我取来。我本以为，我可以这般幸福美满的过一生。
但那日父亲远行归来，一切都变了。他带回了一个同我一般大的女子，并一改往日的和颜悦色。他告诉我，这个名叫白羽的女子，才是他亲生的女儿，而我，不过是府里一个肮脏的下人的孩子。那下人为了让自己的孩子过上好日子，李代桃僵，才让我偷来了这十几年的好时光。
我不信。我用尽办法证明，却只是闹出一场又一场的笑话。而爹爹看在过去的情分上，没有赶走我。但他看我的眼神越来越冷漠。
而在我生辰那日，不，那兴许已经称不上是我的生辰了。府里张灯结彩，都在为上官家真正的嫡小姐祝贺。而我被丢弃，无人问津。但白羽找到我，她穿着上好的华服，贴着精致的妆容，她享有了我曾经拥有的一切。但她看着却不高傲。她那么温和，又有些哀伤。她告诉我，她也不愿看我如此境遇。她劝我在宴席上好好表现，适时她再开口求情，兴许父亲会念在过去的情分上，重新好好待我。
我信了她的话……但那场宴席却成了一场灾难。我费尽心思做成的糕点，竟差点害死了白羽。父亲看着奄奄一息的白羽，终于再也不能容我。他将我赶出了上官家。我成了街头惹人厌弃的老鼠，无处可去。行至那枯井边的时候，我心想，也许那才是我的结局。
但这个时候，那个叫阿笙的男人，抓住了我。
en:
I should have died that day.

Before that day, I was the cherished daughter of the most renowned merchant family in Jiangnan, the favored young mistress of the Shangguan household.
My father cradled me in the palm of his hand, granting my every wish. Even if I had asked for the moon, he would have tried to fetch it for me.
I truly believed I would live out my life in such bliss.

One day, my father returned home from a journey, and everything changed. He brought back a girl my age, and from that moment on, he was no longer the man I knew. He told me that this girl, named Bai Yu, was his true daughter, and that I was merely the child of a lowly servant. That servant, seeking a better life for her own child, had swapped me into the family. The happy years I had stolen... were never truly mine.

I refused to believe it. I tried everything to prove my place, only to make a fool of myself again and again. Father did not cast me out immediately after all these years we lived together. But the warmth that was once in his eyes had turned to cold glances.

On my birthday, though perhaps it no longer belonged to me. The house was adorned with lanterns and banners, all to celebrate the true young mistress of the Shangguan family. Meanwhile, I was left abandoned and forgotten. Bai Yu found me, she stood before me in splendid robes and delicate makeup, draped in everything that once belonged to me. Yet she was not arrogant. She was gentle, yet tinged with sorrow. She said she could not bear to see me so pitiful, urged me to behave well at the banquet. If I did, she would plead on my behalf, and perhaps Father, remembering the past, might show me kindness once more.

I believed her. But the banquet became a nightmare. The pastries I had thoughtfully prepared nearly killed Bai Yu. As Father stared at his dying daughter, all the tolerance he had left for me is gone. He expelled me from the Shangguan household. I became nothing more than a rat in the streets, shunned and despised. With nowhere to go, I wandered to the edge of a dry well, thinking perhaps that was where my story should end.

But it was then that a man named A'Sheng got hold of me.
Sheng Lu

太平钟楼下，敲钟老人的箫声依旧。你的到来并未打断他的闲情。箫声一转，如泣如诉。你不是第一次来到这里，但这一次，你似乎听出了曲中的故事。那是汤汤洛水与皓皓白雪的交锋，是凛冽寒梅与清澈深泉的对望，是一对恋人变作怨侣的转折，是情与义落下至真至痛的一笔，是从此天涯陌路人的诀别。你知道故事里的人是谁，可那场大战她从没对你提起，你也不知最后是谁赢了。老人似乎看出你所想，将同样的问题抛给了你。你思索片刻，回答道……

老人微笑，不置可否。他向你缓缓讲述着故事的余料。悬剑之义，天泉之义，洛神之义，燕北盟之义……每个人都站在了道义的箭锋之上，而引弦之手，从不由人。
en:
Beneath the Peace Bell Tower, the old bell-ringer's flute still sings as ever. Your arrival does nothing to disturb his quiet ease. Then the melody shifted, weeping and whispering like a grief too deep for words. This is not your first time here, yet this time, you seem at last to hear the story hidden within the song.
It is the clash between the surging Luo River and the gleaming white snow; the silent gaze between bitter winter plum and a deep, clear spring. It is the turning point where lovers become estranged, the stroke where love and duty leave their truest, most agonizing mark, the final parting that leaves them as strangers at the ends of the earth. You know who the story is about. Yet she has never spoken of that great battle, and you never learned who emerged victorious in the end. The old man seems to read your thoughts, tossing the same question back to you. After a moment's reflection, you give your answer...
#YThe woman won. Only after leaving Blissful Retreat did you realize the true weight and glory of Aunt Han's title as Water Lady. For so many years, you had been kept safely sheltered beneath her wings. You believed in her martial prowess, the Fleeting Glimpse of Water Lady, swift as a startled swan, which had never been defeated.#E
The old man only smiles, neither confirming nor denying it. Slowly, he recounts the untold fragments of the tale: the honor of the Hanging Blade, the honor of Well of Heaven, the honor of Water Lady, the honor of the Northern Vow… Each stood balanced upon the arrowhead of honor, yet the hand that drew the bowstring was never their own.

zh:
天落雨了。
午时尚且天晴，不过飨食片刻，天就暗了。凉风夹杂雨丝吹来一丝潮意。
客栈内人声鼎沸，一墙之隔，屋外针雨落叶，一方天地只剩雨声。
兰澳站在廊下，正盯着雨幕，视线里出现一只抓着伞的手。
她回过头，看见的就是一脸爽朗傻笑的方白。

后来，兰澳的影子就从一道变成一双。

方白从不遮掩。
他与兰澳一起时，总是围着兰澳转悠，嘴里絮叨不停，尽是些“爱”、“欢喜”、“想”之类的词，毫不避讳，大大方方。
兰澳乍听总是有些恼，时间一长，她却有些习惯，习惯了这样的方白，也习惯不再一人。
每日晨起时，兰澳床边总有一杯温热的白水。方白不知她何时会醒，却总能让水不凉。
她远行时，他从不问她去向，他只问何时归家。当她晚归时，方白都会在黑夜中掌着灯等候。
只要看到兰澳的身影，他就奋力挥手，从疾走到耐不住奔跑，带着跳跃火光，穿过黑暗朝她奔来。
还有那把梳蓖。方白用黄杨木做梳，从兰澳发间轻轻穿过。一梳梳到尾，一顺顺情浓。
他说，他真想与她相守，共梳至白头。
兰澳曾想过，就这样不管不顾，告诉他身上的毒。
但她不敢赌，她也不愿赌。她只能在日复一日的惶恐偷享幸福，直至避无可避。
“啪啦。”
燃烛已尽。
兰澳回神，攥紧手中梳蓖。
这是当初她与方白告别时，下意识带走的物件。
en:
The sky opened up with rain.
At midday, the sun still shone bright, but after a quick bite, the heavens darkened. A cool breeze carried a fine mist of raindrops, weaving a gentle, damp chill through the air.
Inside the bustling inn, voices rose and fell in lively chatter. Yet just beyond the walls, rain pierced falling leaves, and the world outside shrank to the soft patter of droplets.
Lan Ao stood beneath the sheltered porch, her gaze lost in the silken veil of rain. Through the haze, a hand emerged, clutching a humble umbrella.
She turned, and there was Fang Bai, his face radiant with an open, carefree smile.
From then on, Lan Ao's shadow no longer walked alone.

Fang Bai never once concealed his feelings. Whenever they were together, he circled her like a moth drawn to light, rambling on with words like "love," "adore," and "miss," never holding back.
At first, Lan Ao would get a bit huffy. But over time, she grew used to this relentless warmth, and with it, to the quiet comfort of no longer being alone.
Each morning, when Lan Ao awoke, a warm cup of water awaited quietly by her bedside. Fang Bai never knew the exact moment she would rise, yet he always made sure it was never cold.
When she ventured afar, he never asked about her destination, only when she would return home. If she was late, he would wait in the dark with a lantern held high.
The instant her silhouette appeared, he'd wave wildly, his walk breaking into a jog, then a full run, his eyes bright with flickering light. 

And then, there was the comb. One stroke to the end, and love flows with the grain. He whispered that he longed to comb each other's hair until they were grey and old.

Lan Ao had once considered throwing it all away, just telling him about the poison in her blood. But she dared not take that gamble. She wasn't ready to risk it. All she could do was steal scraps of happiness from her daily dread, until there was no escape left.

"Sizzle." The candle burned to its end. Lan Ao snapped out of it, her fingers tightening around the comb. It was the one thing she'd taken without thinking when she walked away from him.

【颜渊第十二】

颜渊问仁，子曰：“克己复礼为仁。一日克己复礼，天下归仁焉。为仁由己，而由人乎哉？”颜渊曰：“请问其目。”子曰：“非礼勿视，非礼勿听，非礼勿言，非礼勿动。”颜渊曰：“回虽不敏，请事斯语矣。”
仲弓问仁，子曰：“出门如见大宾，使民如承大祭，己所不欲，勿施于人。在邦无怨，在家无怨。”仲弓曰：“雍虽不敏，请事斯语矣。”
司马牛问仁。子曰：“仁者，其言也讱也。”曰：“其言也讱，斯可谓之仁已矣乎？”子曰：“为之难，言之得无讱乎？”
司马牛问君子。子曰：“君子不忧不惧。”曰：“不忧不惧，斯可谓君子已乎？”子曰：“内省不疚，夫何忧何惧？”
司马牛忧，曰：“人皆有兄弟，我独亡。”子夏曰：“商闻之矣：死生有命，富贵在天。君子敬而无失，与人恭而有礼，四海之内，皆为兄弟也。君子何患乎无兄弟也？”
子张问明。子曰：“浸润之譛，肤受之诉，不行焉，可谓明也已矣。浸润之譛，肤受之诉，不行焉，可谓远也已矣。”
子贡问政。子曰：“足食，足兵，使民信之矣。”子贡曰：“必不得已而去，于斯三者何先？”曰：“去兵。”曰：“必不得已而去，于斯二者何先？”曰：“去食。自古皆有死，民不信不立。”
棘子城曰：“君子质而已矣，何以文为矣子”贡曰：“惜乎，夫子之说君子也，驷不及舌。文犹质也，质犹文也。虎豹之鞟，犹犬羊之鞟也。
哀公问于有若曰：“年饥，用不足，如之何？”有若对曰：“盍彻乎？”曰：“二，吾犹不足，如之何其彻也？”对曰：“百姓足，君孰与不足？百姓不足，君孰与足？”
子张问崇德、辨惑。子曰：“主忠信，徙义，崇德也。爱之，欲其生也。恶之，欲其死也。既欲其生，又欲其死，是惑。‘诚不以富，亦祗以异。’”
齐景公问政于孔子，孔子对曰：“君君，臣臣，父父，子子。公曰：“善哉！信如君不君，臣不臣，父不父，子不子，虽有粟，吾岂得而食诸？”
子曰：“片言可以折狱者，其由也与！”子路无宿诺。
子曰：“听讼，吾犹人也，必也使无讼乎？”

[Chapter 12: Yan Yuan]

Yan Yuan asked about perfect virtue. The Master said, "To subdue oneself and return to propriety, is perfect virtue. If one can for one day subdue oneself and return to propriety, all under heaven will ascribe perfect virtue to one. Is the practice of perfect virtue from oneself, or is it from others?" Yan Yuan said, "I beg to ask the steps of that process." The Master replied, "Look not at what is contrary to propriety; listen not to what is contrary to propriety; speak not what is contrary to propriety; make no movement which is contrary to propriety." Yan Yuan then said, "Though I am deficient in intelligence and vigour, I will make it my business to practise this lesson."
Zhonggong asked about perfect virtue. The Master said, "It is, when you go abroad, to behave to everyone as if you were receiving a great guest; to employ the people as if you were assisting at a great sacrifice; not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself; to have no murmuring against you in the country, and none in the family." Zhonggong said, "Though I am deficient in intelligence and vigour, I will make it my business to practise this lesson."
Sima Niu asked about perfect virtue. The Master said, "The person of perfect virtue is cautious and slow in one's speech." "Cautious and slow in one's speech!" said Niu; "is this what is meant by perfect virtue?" The Master said, "When one feels the difficulty of doing, can one be other than cautious and slow in speaking?"
Sima Niu asked about the superior person. The Master said, "The superior person has neither anxiety nor fear." "Being without anxiety or fear!" said Niu; "does this constitute what we call the superior person?" The Master said, "When internal examination discovers nothing wrong, what is there to be anxious about, what is there to fear?"
Sima Niu, full of anxiety, said, "Other people all have their brothers, I only have not." Zixia said to him, "There is the following saying which I have heard:— 'Death and life have their determined appointment; riches and honours depend upon Heaven.' Let the superior person never fail reverentially to order one's own conduct, and let one be respectful to others and observant of propriety—then all within the four seas will be one's brothers. What has the superior person to do with being distressed because one has no brothers?"
Zizhang asked what constituted intelligence. The Master said, "One with whom neither slander that gradually soaks into the mind, nor statements that startle like a wound in the flesh, are successful, may be called intelligent indeed. Yea, one with whom neither soaking slander, nor startling statements, are successful, may be called far-seeing."
Zigong asked about government. The Master said, "The requisites of government are that there be sufficiency of food, sufficiency of military equipment, and the confidence of the people in their ruler." Zigong said, "If it cannot be helped, and one of these must be dispensed with, which of the three should be foregone first?" "The military equipment," said the Master. Zigong again asked, "If it cannot be helped, and one of the remaining two must be dispensed with, which of them should be foregone?" The Master answered, "Part with the food. From of old, death has been the lot of all people; but if the people have no faith in their rulers, there is no standing for the state."
Ji Zicheng said, "In a superior person it is only the substantial qualities which are wanted—why should we seek for ornamental accomplishments?" Zigong said, "Alas! Your words, sir, show you to be a superior person, but four horses cannot overtake the tongue. Ornament is as substance; substance is as ornament. The hide of a tiger or leopard stript of its hair, is like the hide of a dog or goat stript of its hair."
Duke Ai inquired of You Ruo, saying, "The year is one of scarcity, and the returns for expenditure are not sufficient—what is to be done?" You Ruo replied to him, "Why not simply tithe the people?" "With two tenths," said the duke, "I find them not enough—how could I do with that system of one tenth?" You Ruo answered, "If the people have plenty, their prince will not be left to want alone. If the people are in want, their prince cannot enjoy plenty alone."
Zizhang having asked how virtue was to be exalted, and delusions to be discovered, the Master said, "Hold faithfulness and sincerity as first principles, and be moving continually to what is right—this is the way to exalt one's virtue. You love a person and wish one to live; you hate one and wish one to die. Having wished one to live, you also wish one to die. This is a case of delusion. 'It may not be on account of her being rich, yet you come to make a difference.'"
Duke Jing of Qi asked Confucius about government. Confucius replied, "There is government, when the prince is prince, and the minister is minister; when the father is father, and the son is son." "Good!" said the duke; "if, indeed, the prince be not prince, the minister not minister, the father not father, and the son not son, although I have my revenue, can I enjoy it?"
The Master said, "Ah! it is You, who could with half a word settle litigations!" Zilu never slept over a promise.
The Master said, "In hearing litigations, I am like any other body. What is necessary, is to cause the people to have no litigations."

Long ago, emissaries traveled by post to Annan, Lang, and Gun prefectures. Carrying instruments to measure the sun's shadow. 
Mount Baima and Mount Taiyue once marked the old Yellow River lands. Through the movement of the shadow can one tell when the tides would rise or fall. 
They say: "To view the heavens through a tube, to measure the sea with a ladle. Such things were never meant to be fully grasped." 
If we try to measure the vastness of heaven and earth with mere sticks and strings, can we ever truly understand their scale? And if we can't, then how vast could they truly be?

zh:
那自称女侠的女子看着升起的铁花，竟和一群小孩一同欢呼雀跃起来，没半点高手风范。
少年苍在一旁睁大眼睛望着她，思索着谁也不知道的事情。
“苍”这个名字，是女子抓耳挠腮，苦思三日后给他取的。当时她叽里咕噜念了一大堆，他只记得好像是有关染色什么的。这名字他没说要，也没说不要；女子也并不在意他要还是不要，喊过来喊过去，就真成了他的名字。
铁花似是看够了，女子伸了个懒腰，苍立马冲到她跟前：
“现在该教我武功了吧！”
女子挠了挠头：“哦，没呢。”而后场中那铁花复又升起，到精彩处她仍是雀跃鼓掌。
“铁花你不感兴趣，庙会里还有别的好玩的。我给你两吊钱，你自己去转转？”
“不要，我要跟你学武功。”
“那么多戏具玩物，就没一个喜欢的？我在你这年纪，一天要玩坏师兄三十个机关呢……”
“不要，我要跟你学武功。”
“嗯……看来还是力气太多，上山去抓头野猪回来，夜晚吃野猪肉。”
“好！等我回来了，教我武功！”
一身蛮劲的少年依言一头钻进了山里，夜里当真背着一头野猪回到了二人借住的道观。之前出手劫道，是他输给了女子，那么按照他心中弱肉强食的道理，要杀要剐，随她心情，他绝不会逃。
吃着野猪肉，少年鼻孔喷着白气，死死盯着女子：
“你不该这么强。”
她确实不该这么强的！她不够狠辣，不够决绝，她毫无危机感！几次出手，或为路边叫花子，或为病弱老大娘，或为开解街边顽童争斗……全是些没有收益的事情！而他自小在街头摸爬滚打，靠着强壮的体魄抢食长大，他知道活下来的规则！
弱者死，强者才能活！他要更强，更强，更强！
女子望着眼前，被磨去欢喜，磨去憎恶，只剩变强执念，或者说——只剩求生本能的弟子，良久后，轻柔地拍了拍他的头：
“可以不着急变强的。未来，一定可以不着急变强的。”
后来师父教给了他武艺，后来师父离开了道观，后来苍去学会了打铁花。
他仍旧不清楚这技艺的用处——打出铁水烫伤自己，让别人欢呼几句；铁水也只闪耀一瞬，而后就变回灰扑扑的渣子。一切似乎毫无意义，但他仍旧一次又一次打出那绚烂的火花，克服直面烈火的恐惧，思索着让师父强大的、不同于弱肉强食的真正道理。
en:
The woman who called herself a heroine watched the iron sparks fly and started cheering right along with the children, with not a trace of a true master about her.
The boy called Goshawk stood off to the side, staring at her with wide eyes and thinking thoughts no one else knew.

She was the one who had given him that name. She had spent three whole days scratching her head over it. At the time, she had rambled on and on about all sorts of things, dyes, birds, and who knew what else. He did not remember much beyond that.

He had never said whether he wanted the name or not. She had never cared whether he did. She kept calling him that, and before long it simply became his name.

When she seemed to have had her fill of the iron sparks, she stretched lazily. Goshawk immediately rushed over to her.

"Now will you teach me martial arts or not?"
She scratched her head. "Nope, not yet."

Then the iron sparks rose again, and when the show reached its best part, she was right back to clapping and cheering.

"If you don't care for this, there are plenty of other fun things at the fair. I'll give you some money. Go have a look around."
"No. I want to learn martial arts."
"With all these toys and tricks here, there's really nothing you like? When I was your age, I could wreck thirty of my senior brother's contraptions in a day..."
"No. I want to learn martial arts."
"Hm... sounds like you've still got too much strength to spare. Go up the mountain and catch a wild boar. We'll have boar tonight."
"Fine. When I get back, you teach me."

The boy, all brute strength and stubbornness, plunged straight into the mountains. That night, he really did return to the daoist temple where they were staying, a whole wild boar slung across his back.

The last time they had crossed paths, he had tried to rob her and lost. By the law he believed in, the strong ate the weak. So if she wanted to kill him or cut him down, that was up to her. He would never run.

As he ate the boar meat, white breath huffing from his nose in the cold, he stared hard at her.

"You shouldn't be this strong."
She really should not have been. She was not ruthless enough, not hard enough, not nearly wary enough. Every time she made a move, it was for something with nothing to gain from it at all: a beggar by the roadside, a sick old granny, some street kids fighting.

None of it brought her anything.

He had grown up scrambling through the streets, snatching food by force because he was stronger than the next person. He knew the rule for staying alive.

The weak died, so the strong could live.
He wanted to be stronger. Stronger. Stronger still.

She looked at the disciple before her, a boy whose joy had been worn away, whose hatred had been worn away too, until all that was left was the need to grow stronger, or rather, the bare instinct to survive.

After a long while, she gently patted him on the head.

"You don't have to be in such a hurry to grow strong. Someday, you really won't have to."

Later, Master taught him martial arts. Later, Master left the daoist temple. Later still, Goshawk learned how to perform iron sparks.

Even then, he still did not really understand what use the craft had.

You flung molten iron into the air and risked burning yourself, just to earn a few cheers. The blaze lasted only an instant before falling back into dull gray slag.

It all seemed meaningless.

And yet he still sent those brilliant sparks flying again and again, learning to face fire without fear, searching for the real truth behind his master's strength, something different from the old law of the strong devouring the weak.
Gou Cehua
Zhu Youli Right Dodge
Xiaozhan

zh:
鬼市多怪人，鬼医涂山允在其中，算不得起眼。
他也不想起眼。
如果可以，他愿永远蜷于那巨大的兜帽下，将自己的脸和身体，乃至自己的一生，全数藏起来。

他生来就是个见不得光的孩子。产婆接过他的时候，发出了惊恐的叫声。他赤红的双眼，遍布全身的白毛，都被村里的人视作某种不祥的预兆。他的父亲远远避开他，他的母亲想救他，却毫无办法。于是没过几天，他就被扔在了村子十里外的河道里，随着水流飘啊飘，不知该去往何方。而这初降的不祥，竟预示了他的一生。

载着他的竹篮在下游被人截住，而那双托起他的手，将他带向了一场万劫不复。
他成了戏团团长的孩子，也成了一个被豢养在笼中供贵人取乐的怪物。
在好些年里，面对那些人或厌弃或好奇或探寻的目光，他都只想躲起来。
他常想，既然他是这样见不得天日的怪物，又为何非要将他曝于天日之下。他就该在黑暗中腐朽，然后死去。

但荣桑水的出现，改变了他本该溃烂的一生。
他被救出，被捡起，被带到了鬼市子。他第一次知道，像他这样的怪人，也能有处可去。
再后来，薛丑花重金寻来良药，竟治好了他大半的伤。有时他在黄泉岸边踱步，看着自己与常人无异的身体，会觉得恍然。
他开始妄想，也许自己，也可以享有常人的一生？
只是可惜，那些落于他心上的伤，始终无法疗愈。漫漫十年过去，他还是畏惧人的目光，畏惧常人习以为常的一切。
他于是藏身鬼市子，成为了其间的一员。

久病成良医，涂山允如今已成了鬼市子最负盛名的圣手。来寻他的人，或求生，或求死，络绎不绝。
那些人说，涂药师不善言辞、不近人情、不喜与人相交，真是个怪人。
涂山允对此甚是满意。他需要那些面具，来掩去他晦暗的过去，与溃烂无可修缮的内里。
en:
The Ghostlight Market is full of oddities, and ghost Physician Tushan Yun was hardly remarkable.
Nor did he wish to be.
If possible, he would have spent eternity hunched beneath his oversized hood, concealing his face, his body, even his entire existence.

He was born a child of shadow. The midwife screamed in horror upon holding him: his crimson eyes and snow-white fur were seen as omens of doom. His father recoiled; his mother tried to save him but failed. Days later, he was abandoned in a river ten miles from the village, drifting aimlessly, his first taste of misfortune, a portent of all that followed.

The bamboo basket carrying him was intercepted downstream, and the hands that lifted him plunged him into a living hell.
He became the circus master's "child", a caged monster for the amusement of nobles.
For years, under their disgusted, curious, probing stares, he longed only to vanish. If I am such a creature of darkness, he often thought, why force me into the light? Let me rot and die unseen.

But Rong Sangshui changed what should have been a festering end.
Rescued, gathered up, brought to the Ghostlight Market, for the first time, he learned that even freaks like him had a place. Later, Xue Chou paid a fortune for medicines that healed most of his scars. Sometimes, walking the riverbank, he would stare at his now-ordinary reflection and feel dazed.
He began to wonder: Could I live a normal life?
But the wounds on his soul refused to heal. A decade on, he still flinched from human eyes, from the mundane world's every touch. So he remained in the Ghostlight Market, becoming one of its own.

Years of suffering forged him into a healer. Now, Tu Shanyun is the most renowned doctor in the Ghostlight Market, sought by those desperate to live... or die.
They call him Physician Tu, cold, averse to company, a strange man.
Tu Shanyun found this reputation deeply satisfying. He needed those masks, to bury his wretched past, and the rot festering beneath.

暖砚是为防冬季墨汁冻结而设计出的砚台，最早可追溯到唐代。唐宋时期，暖砚主要为两层结构，即一层供暖保温，一面置墨。
暖砚的具体样式根据其不同的供暖方式，主要分为水暖型与火暖型两种。顾名思义，水暖型便是借助灌入其夹层中的热水来保温，而火暖型则是在暖砚下层燃烧炭火以达到快速升温的目的。
en:
A warming inkstone was designed to keep ink from freezing in winter, with examples dating back to the Tang dynasty. In the Tang and Song periods, it was typically built in two layers: an upper surface for grinding ink and a lower chamber for heat.
Two main types were common. Water-warmed models held hot water in the inner cavity for steady warmth, while fire-warmed models heated quickly by burning charcoal beneath the stone.

zh:
那一天，我也在。
我们老家有句话，只有死绝了的人，没有死绝了的买卖。
仗打输了又如何，断剑能熔，玉佩能当，铠甲背回去，我擦擦血，还不是和新的一样。若再救起一两个，这辈子都得认我做恩人！这买卖，傻子才不去捞。
但我也知道，能摸到一两把好剑，留条命回来，就算发财了，可不能多贪。

赶到滹沱河北边，天下雨了，铁锈和土腥味儿混在一起，一股死气，不好闻。我瞧着那些尸首，想起自己也杀过人，虏人，用的还是把柴刀。杀人其实很难，人的脖子比想象中硬，手却比想象中软……算了，不说这个。
刚要弯腰扒拉，我瞥见远处还有人站着，一身晋军铠甲立在雨里，威风是威风，却僵得古怪。
没等细看，江晏就来了。我赶紧趴低，早前他就饶过我一次，若知道我还在干这营生，估计麻烦了。他从雨里走来，手里还握着那把梅花宝剑。我记得这把剑，上好的精铁，漂亮得很，要是能被我摸去………大人物的活路总比我多，对吧？要怪就怪这世道艰难，我还有两张嘴巴要喂。
我盯着那把剑，等一个可乘之机。
他走近了些，顺着他的步子往前看，这才看清远处那张脸——眼睛睁得极大，眼仁却灰了，脸上还蒙着一层僵青，比我身边这些断了气的都要渗人。这人，总觉着在哪见过。
想起来了，之前在老家，街上闹哄哄的，人人涌出来看英雄。我也踮脚望过一眼——是王清！……义士敬重的大侠、百姓仰仗的将军，王清？

正想着，剑出鞘了。
一把剑，从不会无故出鞘。可如今，却是宝剑斩英雄。我吓得差点压不住身子！都说江晏出剑极快，想杀一人，无须十步。可眼下他提着剑，走得太慢。
雨砸在地上，好多好多声。二人之间，终是只剩五步。
江晏提着剑迈出第一步，王清将军颤了下，抬起了头，瞧着终于有了些人气。
第二步，我听见嗬嗬声，不知从哪儿传来的，越来越急，像喘不过气。又见将军的脖子里，似是有团青灰色的影子。
第三步，将军的铠甲裂开了……我明白过来，确实不能再等，再等下去，就没有王清将军了。江晏，是为这个而来。可这一剑下去，将军是保住了，江晏呢？
第四步，江晏举起了剑，举得真慢。不知怎么的，透过雨我竟看得更清——名声再大的侠客，到底还是个少年人。我也头回见到杀人者的脸上，没有快意、没有狰狞，只有没法遮掩的悲恸。剑随心动，他的剑，不稳。
第五步，将军也动了。他用尽全力，只让自己往前迈了一步，好让江晏的剑递出去，刚好能钻进心口。至于他靠近他，说了什么，我拼命听，却被雨声盖过……只觉这一剑，不像杀人，更像是把什么东西，轻轻交待了。

王清将军倒下，大雨瓢泼。
原来杀人这件事，也分三六九等。
有的人杀人，靠骗、靠阴、靠背后捅刀，杀完，自己也成了鬼。
有的人杀人，不惜把自己身上最干净的那块地方，也连带着亲手切下来。
杀完，还是英雄。

雨打在脸上，又咸又涩，眼前一下什么都看不清了。只瞧见江晏越走越远，变成一个小点。他之后要去哪，怎么走，我再不知道。而我呢，一个在死人堆里扒拉的混账，不知怎的，一时间怎么也爬不起来。那一天的雨，太重了。
过了好久，我终于能爬起来，经过王清将军时，又看了一眼那柄剑，确实漂亮。我现在就可以摸走这把英雄剑，倒手出去，换下半辈子的荣华富贵……这样想着，我伸出手，弯下腰。

新拾的这柄小木剑，握在手里不过寸长，又圆又钝，柄上系着的平安结，也被血重新染红。
真贪心，都来战场了还揣着这个。
这样也好。
我把它藏进怀里。天还阴着，雨还没停。
en:
I was there that day.
Where I come from, we say there's no such thing as a dead trade until every last trader is dead.
So what if the battle was lost? Broken swords can be melted down. Jade can be pawned. Armor can be cleaned and sold again. Pull a few wounded men out while you're at it, and they'll call you their savior for the rest of their lives. Only a fool leaves a battlefield empty-handed.
That said, even I knew not to push my luck. If I could come away with a good blade or two and keep breathing, that was good enough.

By the time I reached the north bank of the Hutuo River, rain had started falling. The air smelled of rust, wet dirt, and death. I looked over the bodies and remembered I'd killed men myself before, the foreign invaders, with nothing grander than a woodcutter's knife. People talk as if killing is simple. It isn't. A man's neck is tougher than it looks, and your own hand is softer than you'd think. Never mind that.
I was just about to start picking through the dead when I noticed someone still standing in the rain. He wore Jin armor and stood straight as a spear, but something about him was wrong. Too still. Too stiff.
Then Jiang Yan appeared. I dropped flat immediately. He had spared me once before, and if he caught me still making a living this way, I doubted he'd do it twice. He came through the rain with that plum-blossom sword in his hand. Fine steel. Beautiful blade. If I could get hold of it... well, great men always have more ways to live than the likes of me. Hard times are hard times, and I still had mouths to feed.
So I watched the sword and waited for my chance.
As Jiang Yan came closer, I finally got a clear look at the man in front of him. His eyes were wide open, but the pupils had gone gray. His face had turned a dead blue. He looked worse than the bodies at my feet. Even so, I knew that face.
Then I remembered. Back home once, the whole street had turned out to catch a glimpse of a hero. I'd done the same. It was Wang Qing. The man righteous folk admired, the general ordinary people trusted. That Wang Qing.

And then Jiang Yan drew his sword.
A sword does not leave the sheath for no reason. But seeing a good blade raised against a hero nearly made me break cover. People said Jiang Yan could kill a man in fewer than ten steps. That day, though, he walked so slowly it hurt to watch.
The rain hammered the ground between them. Five steps remained.
On the first step, General Wang shuddered and raised his head. For a moment, he looked almost alive again.
On the second, I heard a wet rasping sound. I couldn't tell where it was coming from. Then I saw something gray-blue moving in his throat.
On the third, his armor split open. That was when I understood. If Jiang Yan waited any longer, there would be nothing left of Wang Qing to save. That was why he had come. But if he drove that sword home, what would be left of Jiang Yan?
On the fourth, Jiang Yan raised the blade. Slowly. Too slowly. And somehow, through the rain, I saw him more clearly than ever. No matter how famous a swordsman becomes, he can still just be a young man. I had never seen a killer's face look like that before. There was no thrill in it. No rage. Only grief. A sword follows the heart, and his heart was shaking. So was the blade.
Then came the fifth step. General Wang moved first. With everything he had left, he stepped forward just enough to meet the sword himself, just enough to guide it into his own heart. He leaned in and said something to Jiang Yan. I strained to hear it, but the rain swallowed every word. All I knew was this: it did not look like murder. It looked like one man placing something precious into another man's hands.

Then General Wang fell, and the rain came down harder still.
That was the day I learned there are different kinds of killing.
Some men kill with tricks, ambushes, and knives in the back. By the time they are done, they've turned themselves into ghosts.
Some men kill by cutting away the cleanest part of their own heart with their own hand. And when it's over, they are still heroes.

The rain stung my face. Everything blurred. I watched Jiang Yan walk away until he was no more than a speck. Where he went after that, I never knew. As for me, a bastard who made his living picking through the dead, I could not get up for the longest time. The rain that day felt too heavy to stand under.
Much later, I finally forced myself up. As I passed General Wang, I looked at that sword again. It really was a beautiful thing. I could take it, sell it, and buy myself comfort for the rest of my life. That was what I was thinking when I bent down and reached out.

What I picked up instead was a tiny wooden sword, barely a handspan long. Round, blunt, childish. A little good-luck knot still hung from the hilt, stained red with blood.
Greedy little thing. Came to a battlefield and still brought this along.
Maybe that was for the best.
I tucked it inside my coat. The sky was still dark, and the rain still had not stopped.

武德二年，江湖通缉钱妙手，于灞陵之畔。其时月上高天，江湖高手尽围钱妙手于绝地。忽听钱妙手高呼“摄星拿月”，众人只觉手中兵器空空，忽又见天地昏暗无边，竟是天上之月被一团黑影吞噬不见。

没人知道钱妙手最后去了哪里，有人说，他后来归隐龙王寨，有人说，他早已消逝人间。但后来的后来，他的那手摄星拿月的绝技，却从江湖中传出来。

en:
【Seasonal Rhythms · Part Two】

【Autumn】

Mountain Dwelling in an Autumn Dusk
Wang Wei
After fresh rain in empty hills, the air turns crisp as autumn nears.
Bright moonbeams pierce the pines; clear streams flow over stones.
From bamboo groves, laughter of washerwomen returning home; lotus leaves stir as fishing boats glide down.
Let spring's fragrant blooms fade as they will; here, a noble recluse may choose to stay.

Ode to Autumn
Liu Yuxi
Since ancient times, autumn brings thoughts of loneliness and sorrow,
But I say autumn days outshine the dawn of spring.
A single crane soars through clouds against a clear blue sky,
Inspiring poetic thoughts that reach the azure heights.

Chant by the River at Dusk
Bai Juyi
A streak of fading sunlight spreads upon the water,
Half the river shimmers green, half glows crimson red.
How lovely is the night of the third day, ninth moon—
Dewdrops gleam like pearls, the crescent moon hangs like a bow.

Mountain Journey
Du Mu
Far up the cold mountain, a stone path winds askew,
Where white clouds dwell deep, there lies a household or two.
I halt my carriage, enchanted by maple woods at dusk,
Frost-reddened leaves outshine the flowers of early spring.

【Winter】

Recalling the Hermit Hu's Home on a Snowy Winter Evening
Wang Wei
Cold night-watches pass; dawn's arrow sounds the hour.
In a clear mirror, I behold my aging face.
Beyond the window, wind startles the bamboo;
Opening the door, I find the mountains clad in snow.
Flakes drift through silent, deep lanes;
White accumulation rests on the broad, tranquil courtyard.
I inquire of Yuan An's humble dwelling—
Serenely, his gate remains closed.

Midnight Songs · Winter Song
Li Bai
At dawn the courier will depart;
All night she stuffs the wadding for his campaign robe.
Her fair hands, chilled, draw the needle—
How can she bear the cold of scissors?
She sews and sends it to a distant road;
How many days to reach Lintao?

Winter Solstice
Du Fu
Year after year on this day, I remain a wanderer,
Suddenly, grinding poverty and sorrow torment me.
On the river, my form appears alone and aged;
By heaven's edge, local customs foster kinship of their own.
With a stick of goosefoot, I tread the crimson ravine after snow;
Jade pendants tinkle at court, dispersing from the Purple Palace.
My heart is broken now, not an inch remains whole;
The road is lost—where can I glimpse the land of Three Qins?

Drinking on an Early Winter Night
Du Mu
Ailing in Huaiyang, I seek a moment's solace in wine,
My traveler's sleeves dusted with frost, facing the candle tray.
Below the steps, pear blossoms lie like a heap of snow—
Who will lean on this railing come next year?
Have you come... to deliver me to the other side?
Ruan's Dyehouse - Head Manager

zh:
她差一脚就是一只玄猫了。
玄猫怪猫就差一个字，她多想拥有一个帅气的名字。玄猫，通体乌黑，辟邪之物，祥瑞之征！可她黑得不彻底，生得一只雪白的后腿。非但不祥瑞，反而被视作怪猫了。
她被人赶到村后的大树下，竟和一个躲在那儿恸哭的女人对上了眼。
那女人泪眼汪汪，愣了半晌，迟疑地来扒拉她这只与众不同的猫腿。
毛丫，恁来看俺啦？女人这么说着。
毛丫，这就是她盼星星盼月亮，盼到的帅气名字吗？
一时间不知道要不要反抗。女人见她没有动弹，更是将她挤在了怀里。自己的毛很厚实，可以盛住女人的眼泪。
相处得久了，毛丫看得出，村里的人不太喜欢那个女人。是因为她说话声音很大吗？是因为她总是在夜里哭吗？是因为她捡了自己这只不招人喜欢的猫咪吗？
王秀莲不知道，毛丫偷偷出走过，为了不再给她惹来麻烦。
只是走到村口时，听见一帮人聊闲，说这地儿的人呐，管最宝贝的小子叫孩蛋，最心爱的闺女，都叫毛丫。
毛丫听了，一回头，吧嗒吧嗒地跑回王秀莲的怀里。
这就是她等来的最好的名字。
en:
It was just one step away from being a mystic black cat. There is only a one-word difference between "mystic cat" and "freak cat," and how it longed for a cool title. A mystic black cat, pitch-black all over, wards off evil and brings good omens! But its black coat was incomplete, marred by a single snow-white hind leg. Instead of being an auspicious symbol, it was seen as a freak.

Driven away by the villagers, it ended up under a large tree behind the village, unexpectedly locking eyes with a woman weeping bitterly in the shadows.

The woman, teary-eyed, froze for a long while before hesitantly reaching out to stroke its unusual white leg. "Maoya... my little fluff, did you come to see me?" the woman murmured.

Maoya? Was this the cool name it had been longing for?

For a moment, it did not know whether to resist. Seeing it stay perfectly still, the woman pulled it tightly into her embrace. Its fur was very thick, thick enough to catch the woman's tears.

Over time, it noticed that the villagers did not quite like this woman. Was it because her voice was too loud? Because she always cried at night? Or because she had taken in an unlovable cat like itself?

Wang Xiulian never knew that the cat once snuck away, simply to spare her any more trouble. But just as it reached the village entrance, it overheard some idlers chatting. They said that in this region, folks called their most precious boys "Haidan," their little rascals, and their most beloved daughters "Maoya," their fluffy sweethearts.

Hearing this, it turned right around and trotted briskly back into Wang Xiulian's arms.

It was the best name it could have ever waited for.

zh: 女化蚕，又称蚕女、马头娘，是中国古代一则神话传说，载于东晋干宝的《搜神记》。故事讲述一位少女因思念远征的父亲，对家中牡马戏言，许诺若能迎父归家便嫁其为妻 。马闻言后寻回其父，后因少女之父毁约杀马，曝皮于庭。马皮突然卷起少女飞走，最终两者在一棵树上化为蚕，吐丝作茧。该传说解释了蚕的由来，蚕女也在后来成为民间信仰中的蚕神， 现济南市华阳宫棉花殿内供奉的“棉花娘娘”即为女蚕。
en: The legend of the Lady of Silk, also known as the Horse-Headed Goddess, is a captivating Chinese myth first recorded in the Eastern Jin anthology In Search of the Divine. It tells the story of a young girl who desperately missed her father while he was away at war. In a moment of longing, she jokingly promised the family's stallion that she would marry it if it brought her father home. The horse actually succeeded, but the father, horrified by the vow, broke the promise, slaughtered the stallion, and left its hide in the courtyard to dry. Suddenly, the skin sprang to life, wrapped itself tightly around the girl, and carried her away. They eventually landed in a tree, fusing together into a silkworm that immediately began spinning a cocoon. This myth explains the origins of silk-making, and the maiden was later worshiped as its patron goddess. In fact, the "Cotton Goddess" still enshrined in Cotton Hall of Jinan's Huayang Palace today is actually a representation of this very Lady of Silk.
